item.title: A Syndrome-Extraction Framework for Distributed Lattice Surgery on Arbitrary Rotated Surface-Code Layouts
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Seam construction for distributed lattice surgery maintains minimum CNOT depth of 4, achieves fault distance d−1, and delivers lower, more stable logical error rates than alternating or interleaving schedules under link noise swept from 10p to 100p (with bulk noise p=10−4).

Grade 0.530 · 3.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Pritesh Thakur, Daniel Dilley, Zain Saleem

Figure

Merged rotated surface-code layout for logical Pauli-XX measurement, showing weight-4 stabilizers at module seams split into paired weight-2 checks mediated across the boundary.

Asks

How can distributed lattice surgery merge rotated surface-code patches with arbitrary boundaries across noisy inter-module links while avoiding distance-reducing hook errors and minimizing CNOT depth?

Before

Prior Bell-measurement lattice surgery achieved a fault distance of 3d/4 under noisy bulk conditions (and standard interleaving schedules required larger qubit overheads and higher CNOT depth).

But

Evaluated via circuit-level numerical simulations under uniform depolarizing noise with fixed bulk error rate p=10−4. Requires native three-qubit CXX gates at module seams.

Tools

Bell-state mediated split ancilla checks · Three-qubit native CXX parity measurements · Algebraic detector annotation · Stim quantum circuit simulator

Code. https://github.com/Pritesh402/modular-surgery

Abstract

Modular quantum computing is a leading candidate for scalable fault tolerant quantum computation. Performing lattice surgery using surface code patches in different modules requires the use of inter-module gates that are noisier than the local gates. Furthermore, the merged layouts during lattice surgery expose multiple directions in which hook errors can propagate to reduce the fault distance. Existing hook-avoiding schedules either increase the syndrome extraction circuit depth, or let link faults propagate into the bulk. We introduce a seam construction that allows splitting arbitrary merged rotated surface code layout into smaller patches with uniform boundaries that could keep their own hook-avoiding N/Z shaped schedule. At the seam we split weight-4 stabilizers into pairs of weight-2 stabilizers that are mediated through a Bell pair and measured within a CNOT depth of 4. We also employ the use of three-qubit textttCXX gates for parity measurements at the seam to maintain the minimum CNOT depth. Through this seam construction, we confine the elevated link error at the seam, protecting the bulk from higher error rate. We also give a custom detector annotator for such seams that can find the detector space, annotate detectors in the Stim circuits, and ensure that they are suitable to use by matching decoders. We implement our construction for the logical Pauli-XX measurement lattice surgery and a cross-shaped spatial junction and sweep the link error rate from 10 times to 100 times a fixed bulk error rate, and show that our construction gives the lowest and most stable logical error rate than the other frameworks compared here.

item.title: Error Suppression in Distributed Quantum Computing with Heterogeneous-Distance Lattice Surgery
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Heterogeneous-distance lattice surgery with an enlarged ancilla (dA=2d+1) spanning the inter-QPU boundary achieves logical readout error rates nearly independent of link noise, cutting 5−11−5 physical qubit sites by 28.4% compared to uniform distance-9 (373 vs 521 qubits).

Grade 0.502 · 2.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery” · Daniel Dilley, Anastashia Jebraeilli, Rayat Roy, Shobhit Gupta, Alvin Gonzales, Zain Saleem

Figure

Control-X decoding failure probability per CNOT plotted against physical link error probability plink from 10−3 to 10−2. Heterogeneous 5−11−5 stays nearly flat and matches uniform distance-9 at high link noise while outperforming uniform distance-5 and -7.

Asks

How effectively can additional fault-tolerant error protection be concentrated at a noisy quantum processor interface while preserving the code distance of local data patches?

Before

Uniform distance-3 and distance-5 implementations, which exhibit steep increases in logical error rates as link noise grows; at plink=10−2, heterogeneous 3−7−3 reduces decoding failure by factors of ≈13 and ≈19 relative to uniform distance-3.

But

Evaluated under circuit-level stochastic depolarizing noise with fixed local noise plocal=10−4; excludes idle noise, link-generation latency/failures, leakage, and correlated link faults. Requires more total inter-QPU gate applications despite fewer physical sites.

Tools

Rotated surface codes · 8-DAM (eight-data-patch ancilla-mediated) architecture · Traveling stabilizer syndrome scheduling · Circuit-level Stim simulations

Abstract

Distributed quantum computing requires fault-tolerant operations across inter-QPU links that can be substantially noisier than local gates. Uniformly increasing code distance provides additional protection but also enlarges data patches used for local storage and computation. Here, we introduce distributed heterogeneous-distance lattice surgery using an eight-data-patch ancilla-mediated (8-DAM) architecture, which will be useful for near-term quantum devices with less qubit overhead. In this architecture, the central ancilla spanning the inter-QPU boundary is enlarged while the data patches retain distance d. The protocol uses traveling stabilizers to suppress hook errors during merge and split operations between these unequal-distance patches. Circuit-level simulations of rotated surface codes at fixed local depolarizing noise show that logical-readout error rates depend only weakly on link noise. The resulting advantage over conventional lattice surgery grows as link errors increase. Comparisons with uniform distance implementations demonstrate comparable logical error suppression with reduced physical-qubit overhead. We also demonstrate how 8-DAM layouts support two simultaneous distributed logical CNOT operations between four logical data qubits using a single enlarged ancilla. At higher link noise, this construction yields lower logical error rates and more stability than two independent distributed logical CNOTs. These results support selective ancilla enlargement as a resource-efficient approach to fault-tolerant distributed quantum computing.

item.title: Error Correction Properties of Covariant Bosonic Encodings
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Quantum error correction matrices are morphisms of group representations; Schur's lemma forces error matrix blocks to vanish when the symmetric power of the error representation shares no irreducible component with the codespace representation, reducing Knill-Laflamme conditions to character decomposition checks.

Grade 0.469 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes” · Frederic St-Amand, Jean-Philippe Burelle, Baptiste Royer

Figure

Plots near-optimal infidelity 1−F~ against initial coherent state parameters under the amplitude damping channel with photon loss probability γ=0.095 for the two-mode quaternion code.

Asks

How can finite-group representation theory be used to systematically construct multimode covariant bosonic codes and determine their error-correction capabilities?

But

Analyzes finite subgroups of SU(2) under the amplitude damping channel; predicts error correctability in principle without specifying recovery protocols.

Tools

Jordan-Schwinger map · Finite-group representation theory · Schur's lemma · Knill-Laflamme conditions · Near-optimal fidelity

Abstract

Bosonic codes offer a promising approach towards hardware-efficient fault tolerance, with many leading examples such as the cat-code and the GKP code organized by an underlying symmetry. We build on a representation-theoretic framework of quantum error correction to formalize the construction and analysis of multimode symmetric bosonic codes, focusing on finite groups. Here, a physical, logical representation and an initial seed state together define the codewords via a covariant encoding. A central observation is that QEC matrices can be viewed as morphisms of group representations, so that Schur's lemma forces entire irreducible representations blocks to vanish. We recover several known single- and two-mode bosonic codes and build and analyze the error protection capabilities of three codes based on finite subgroups of SU(2). We analyze the impact of reducibility of the logical representation and optimize the seed state using the near-optimal fidelity.

item.title: Exploring Asymmetric QEC Code Concatenation
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Alternating mixed Hadamard deformations within each concatenation level (`Alternate_Mixed_within_Level`) yields near-identical X and Z logical error rates while minimizing total logical error rate across one to four concatenation levels. Undeformed concatenation exhibits up to a 60× higher Z error rate than X error rate at concatenation level l=4.

Grade 0.458 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes” · Sayam Sethi, Maxwell Poster, Aditi Awasthi, Willers Yang, Joshua Viszlai, Jonathan Mark Baker

Figure

Logical error rate versus physical error rate under unbiased noise across concatenation levels l=1 to 4, comparing total, X, and Z LER and the Z/X error ratio across six deformation strategies.

Asks

How can Clifford deformations balance the asymmetric X and Z syndrome checks and logical error rates in concatenated [[4,1,2]] Iceberg codes?

Before

Undeformed concatenated [[4,1,2]] Iceberg code produced skewed X and Z error rates due to having asymmetric check counts (2×X and 1×Z).

But

Code capacity phenomenological depolarizing noise (unbiased and 8× biased), single-qubit Hadamard deformations only, simulated up to four concatenation levels with 500,000 Monte Carlo shots.

Tools

Hadamard Clifford deformations · Concatenated [[4,1,2]] Iceberg code · Level-by-level soft-information maximum-likelihood decoding · Monte-Carlo error simulations

Abstract

Concatenated quantum error-correcting codes have recently gained popularity because they improve the effective distance of a joint code without requiring the discovery of new codes with desirable parameters. A common building block for such studies is the [[4,1,2]] Iceberg code, the smallest error-detecting code and therefore the one with the lowest resource overhead. However, it has an asymmetric number of X and Z checks, and concatenating it produces skewed logical error rates (LERs) between the X and Z observables. This asymmetry can be mitigated by Clifford-deforming the individual blocks of the concatenation, but the space of possible Hadamard deformations grows doubly exponentially with the number of concatenation levels. We formalize this deformation space and investigate it by proposing six concrete deformation strategies, which we compare under a code capacity (with and without bias) noise model using a concatenated maximum-likelihood soft-information decoder. Among the strategies we study, one one of them achieves near-identical X and Z LERs in a logical-memory experiment while simultaneously reducing the total LER (the sum of the X and Z error rates).

item.title: Transversal non-Clifford gates on good quantum locally testable codes
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Asymptotically good [ ldN, ldΘ(N), ldΘ(N)] qLDPC and qLTC codes with soundness Θ(1) support nontrivial transversal logical Cr−1Z non-Clifford gates for any integer r≥2.

Grade 0.435 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Asymptotically good Quantum and locally testable classical LDPC codes” · Yiming Li, Zimu Li, Zi-Wen Liu

Asks

Can asymptotically good quantum LDPC codes and quantum locally testable codes directly support transversal non-Clifford logical gates simultaneously with linear distance and constant soundness?

Before

Nontrivial transversal logical multi-controlled-Z gates were achieved on almost-good qLDPC codes and qLTCs with polylogarithmic losses in distance and soundness (Li-Li-Liu 2026).

But

Characteristic 2 base fields; odd-sheeted covering towers; asymptotic N→∞ regime.

Tools

arithmetic cubical complexes · projective Reed-Solomon local codes · cup product pairing with sheaf coefficients · covering space transfer map · Moore determinants

Abstract

We achieve nontrivial transversal logical multi-controlled-Z gates with asymptotically optimal parameters simultaneously on quantum low-density parity check codes and quantum locally testable codes, by applying the gate framework of [arXiv:2604.01874] to the recent good qLTC construction of [arXiv:2609.20780]. To this end, we use the covering space method to construct a nonzero cup product pairing on a finite arithmetic cubical complex. This differs from the previous construction of almost-good codes, whose base space is a hypergraph product. We express the pairing as a coefficient in a product of Moore determinants and prove polynomial nonvanishing by a bipartite multigraph specialization. We then construct covering spaces to obtain an asymptotic family of good qLTCs on which the pulled-back pairing induces the desired nontrivial transversal logical action.

item.title: When Quantum Meets AI: Quantum Methods for Machine Learning and Machine Learning Methods for Quantum Systems
item.description:
Worth a look review — Mamba-based surface code decoder matches Transformer accuracy while cutting inference scaling from quartic to quadratic in code distance. Multi-shift stochastic reconfiguration reduces checkpoint-local validation residuals and update variance relative to fixed-shift SR.

Grade 0.417 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Tak Hur

Asks

How can learned representations and statistical control optimize quantum machine learning algorithms and neural network decoders for quantum error correction?

Before

Transformer baseline had quartic inference-cost scaling with code distance.

But

NMR processor demonstration; finite Monte Carlo sampling; additional computational cost for multi-shift SR.

Tools

Neural Quantum Embedding · Deterministic quantum computation with one qubit (DQC1) · NMR quantum processor · Mamba-based neural decoder · Multi-shift stochastic reconfiguration

Abstract

This thesis studies the intersection of quantum computing and artificial intelligence in two directions: quantum methods for machine learning and machine learning methods for quantum systems. For quantum machine learning, Neural Quantum Embedding learns data representations that increase the trace distance between embedded class ensembles, lowering an embedding-dependent bound on empirical risk and improving classification on noisy quantum hardware. A training objective based on the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product extends this approach to deterministic quantum computation with one qubit (DQC1) and is demonstrated on an NMR quantum processor. A margin-based generalization analysis then connects quantum neural network performance to quantum state discrimination. In the studied benchmarks, margin distributions predict generalization more reliably than parameter-count metrics. For quantum systems, a Mamba-based neural decoder for surface codes matches a reproduced Transformer baseline in memory experiments while reducing inference-cost scaling from quartic to quadratic in code distance. Under an explicit decoder-induced-noise model, it achieves lower logical error rates and a higher effective threshold. For neural quantum states, stochastic reconfiguration is interpreted as tangent-space ridge regression, with its diagonal shift controlling the bias-variance trade-off under finite Monte Carlo sampling. Multi-shift stochastic reconfiguration reduces checkpoint-local validation residuals and update variance relative to fixed-shift SR, at additional computational cost. Together, these contributions show how learned representations, statistical control, and hardware constraints shape the exchange between quantum computing and machine learning.

item.title: Strong matchgate designs in nearly optimal depth
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Strong ε-approximate relative error matchgate k-designs can be generated in depth 𝒪(k2rt(𝖦)log⁡nlog⁡(n/ε)) on a graph 𝖦 with routing number rt(𝖦), and exact strong matchgate 3-designs in depth 𝒪(rt(𝖦)log⁡n) without ancillae.

Grade 0.415 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits” · Maxwell West, M. Cerezo, Martin Larocca

Figure

Schematic of the design construction showing generation via random 2-Majorana rotations, compression into parallel non-overlapping commuting layers, and compilation through a fermionic routing permutation.

Asks

Can non-local qubit connectivity enable the formation of matchgate designs in sublinear circuit depth, circumventing the linear-depth barrier present in one-dimensional architectures?

Before

1D nearest-neighbour circuits require Ω(n) depth to form approximate 2-designs over matchgates.

But

Applies to ancilla-free circuits; depth requires connectivity graphs 𝖦 with low routing number (rt(𝖦)=2 for all-to-all connectivity).

Tools

random walks on the matchgate group · fermionic routing algorithm · representation theory of SO(2n) · circuit layer compression

Abstract

Understanding the resources required to generate approximately random unitaries over various groups is a natural goal of quantum information theory. With respect to one notion of approximation, that of a design, it is known that the full unitary group can be approximated in logarithmic depth by one-dimensional circuits of nearest-neighbour 2-local gates. On the other hand, remarkably, circuits with this connectivity cannot form designs over the matchgate group in sublinear depth. Here we show that this dramatic slowdown can disappear when using a general qubit connectivity graph G of routing number rt(G). Indeed, in this setting one can obtain (strong) ε-approximate relative error matchgate k-designs in depth O(k²rt(G)lognlog(n/ε)). For all-to-all connectivity, rt(G)=2. Our construction is conceptually simple, involving a random walk on the matchgate group, and no ancillae. As a technical byproduct, we improve upon the state of the art for fermionic routing, obtaining an O(rt(G)logn) depth router. Additionally, for k=3, we obtain an exact strong matchgate design in O(rt(G)logn) depth, again without ancillae. Under all-to-all connectivity, our fermionic router and 3-designs are optimal. Notably, our results imply that quantum algorithms for fermionic tomography which require drawing from a matchgate 3-design may be exponentially sped up on quantum computers with all-to-all connectivity, relative to their strictly one-dimensional counterparts.

item.title: Good Quantum Locally Testable Codes from Product Expansion
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Explicit quantum locally testable CSS codes over binary alphabet with constant rate, quantum distance, soundness, and locality, conditional on Reed-Solomon product expansion conjecture.

Grade 0.408 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Asymptotically good Quantum and locally testable classical LDPC codes” · Mitali Bafna, Anqi Li, Quynh T. Nguyen

Figure

Schematic of local view at vertex v showing how edge symmetries and coordinate changes map local views into tensor codes via rescaling and permutations.

Asks

Can structured local codes with compatible symmetries overcome the polylogarithmic distance and soundness bottleneck in high-dimensional expander quantum locally testable code constructions?

Before

Almost-good qLTCs with constant rate and locality but inverse-polylogarithmic relative distance and soundness (Dinur, Lin, and Vidick 2023).

But

Conditioned on validity of product expansion conjecture (Conjecture 5.6) for Reed-Solomon codes; asymptotic code family over 𝔽2.

Tools

Dinur-Lin-Vidick HDX framework · Rungtanapirom-Stix-Vdovina 4D non-Abelian cubical complexes · Reed-Solomon local codes · Morgenstern Ramanujan graph spectral bounds

Abstract

We construct quantum locally testable codes (LTCs) with constant rate, distance, soundness and locality under a variant of a product expansion conjecture of Bafna and Vyas about Reed-Solomon codes. In particular, we use the high-dimensional expansion framework of Dinur, Lin and Vidick for constructing quantum LTCs, instantiated with the non-Abelian cubical complexes of Rungtanapirom, Stix and Vdovina. Our code is obtained by equipping the complex with carefully chosen Reed-Solomon local codes whose symmetries are compatible with those of the complex.
